title: The Mellifluous Doctor — Fontaine to Clairvaux
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Dream of Aleth — Fontaine and the Burgundy of his kin

stops.name: Fontaine-lès-Dijon — the castle of his birth
stops.campa: In the castle above the springs north of Dijon, to Tescelin the Tawny and pious Aleth of Montbard, a third son is born. Before his birth Aleth dreams she carries in her womb a white dog with a russet back, and it barks without ceasing. Frightened, she asks a holy man, who tells her the child will be the guardian of God's house and a great preacher, faithful where so many watchdogs are dumb. She rears her sons herself, feeding them plain bread as though already for the cloister. The boy grows fair, quick, and grave, marked from the cradle.
stops.quote: The child who will be born of you will be the guardian of the house of God, and will bark loudly against the enemies of the faith; for he will be an excellent preacher.
stops.quote_source: Vita Prima Bernardi (William of Saint-Thierry), on Aleth's dream
suggested_refs: Château de Fontaine-lès-Dijon, now a church over his birthplace
Vita Prima Sancti Bernardi, Book I

stops.name: Châtillon-sur-Seine — the schools and the boy's studies
stops.campa: Sent to the school of the canons of Saint-Vorles at Châtillon, Bernard drinks in letters and grammar and loves learning with a burning zeal. He is drawn especially to the Virgin, and the story is told that as a child at Christmas, keeping vigil, he sees in a dream the Infant Christ born again before his eyes — a vision he says shaped his whole life. His mother dies while he is still young; grief turns him inward. Handsome, well-born, courted by the world, he feels already the pull of another country, and begins to fear his own gifts.
suggested_refs: Church of Saint-Vorles, Châtillon-sur-Seine
The Christmas vision of the Infant, recounted in his sermons

stops.name: Church of Saint-Bénigne, Dijon — the prayer that seals his vow
stops.campa: Torn between the world and God, riding to his brothers at the siege of Grancey, Bernard turns aside into a wayside church, kneels, and weeps, lifting his hands to heaven and pouring out his heart. He rises resolved: he will renounce all and enter the poorest, hardest house of God. And he will not go alone. He begins at once to preach to his own — brothers, uncle, kinsmen, friends of the Burgundian nobility — with such fire that mothers hide their sons and wives their husbands, for whoever hears Bernard is lost to the world.
suggested_refs: Cathedral of Saint-Bénigne, Dijon
Vita Prima, Book I, on his conversion of his kinsmen

stops.name: Grancey — the siege, and the brothers won over
stops.campa: Bernard goes to his brothers Guy and Gerard at the siege of Grancey and lays before them the choice between the two Jerusalems. Guy, married with children, hesitates, and Bernard tells him his wife will herself take the veil — which she soon does. Gerard the soldier scoffs, until a lance-wound and capture in the very spot Bernard foretold break his heart, and he too yields. One by one the household falls: the uncle Gaudry a valiant knight, the younger brothers Andrew and Bartholomew, friends of the Burgundian court. Only Nivard the child and the old father Tescelin stay behind — for now.
stops.quote: You will be wounded, Gerard, and made captive; but fear not, for you shall be saved. Even now the door is opened to you by which you shall enter religion.
stops.quote_source: Bernard to his brother Gerard (Vita Prima, Book I; recalled in Sermon 26 on the Song of Songs)
suggested_refs: Grancey-le-Château
Blessed Gerard of Clairvaux, mourned in Bernard's Sermon 26

stops.name: Jully-sur-Sarce — the sister Humbeline turns from the world
stops.campa: Humbeline, Bernard's only sister, comes to visit her brothers at their new poverty, arriving in silks and finery with a great retinue. Bernard refuses to see her, calling her a snare of the devil dressed for hell. Stung to the heart, she weeps and asks only to be told how to live; if he commands, she will obey in all things. He bids her forsake her vanities and follow her husband's leave. She strips off the world, and in time enters the nunnery of Jully, becoming prioress and, like her brothers, is numbered among the blessed. The whole house of Tescelin has gone over to God.
suggested_refs: Priory of Jully-les-Nonnains
Blessed Humbeline, sister of Saint Bernard

segments.name: The Thirty into Cîteaux — the New Monastery

stops.name: Cîteaux — the New Monastery, entered with thirty companions
stops.campa: Bernard leads into Cîteaux some thirty men — four of his own brothers, an uncle, kinsmen and friends, all won by his preaching. The New Monastery under Abbot Stephen Harding is a strict experiment in the naked Rule of Benedict: manual labor, plain psalmody, gray undyed wool, no ornament, no surplus. The house had been failing, near to empty, its abbot half-minded to resign; the sudden flood of well-born novices is its resurrection. Bernard embraces the hardest fasts and vigils, so absorbed in God that after a year in the novitiate he cannot say whether the ceiling is vaulted or flat.
stops.quote: We who have left all things for Christ's sake regard as dung, that we may win Christ, whatever shines with beauty, whatever charms the ear with sound, whatever delights the smell.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Apologia ad Guillelmum, on Cistercian austerity
suggested_refs: Abbaye de Cîteaux (Saint-Nicolas-lès-Cîteaux)
The Charter of Charity of Stephen Harding

stops.name: Cîteaux — the novice sealed to God
stops.campa: Through his novice year Bernard so guards his senses that he lives in the cloister a stranger to the world of the body: he crosses the whole church a hundred times and cannot say whether the ceiling is one vault or many, and after a year by the lake at Cîteaux he thinks there is but one window where there are three. He keeps custody of the eyes so strict that riding all day beside a lake he does not know at evening that water was near. To his own soul he puts the one question he says holds his whole life: Bernard, to what end have you come?
stops.quote: Bernard, Bernard, to what purpose have you come here?
stops.quote_source: Bernard's watchword to himself in the novitiate (Vita Prima, Book I)
suggested_refs: Abbaye de Cîteaux
Vita Prima, Book I, on Bernard's custody of the senses

segments.name: The Valley of Wormwood — the founding of Clairvaux

stops.name: Clairvaux — Claire Vallée in the Valley of Wormwood
stops.campa: At twenty-five Bernard is sent out with twelve monks to found a daughter-house. They come to a wild ravine on the left bank of the Aube, the Vallée d'Absinthe — the Valley of Wormwood, a den of robbers — and there raise huts of branches and begin. Hunger comes first: they boil beech-leaves for bread, and Bernard, when the last coin is gone, sends a brother to buy on the strength of God alone. The bitter valley is renamed Clara Vallis, the Bright Valley — Clairvaux. His own austerity ruins his health; only the General Chapter and his friend Bishop William of Champeaux force him to relent.
stops.quote: You will find something more in woods than in books. Trees and stones will teach you that which you can never learn from masters.
suggested_refs: Site of Clairvaux Abbey (later prison), Ville-sous-la-Ferté, Aube
The 1115 foundation manuscripts of Clairvaux

stops.name: Châlons-sur-Marne — ordained and blessed as abbot
stops.campa: Bernard goes to William of Champeaux, Bishop of Châlons, to be ordained priest and blessed as first abbot of Clairvaux. The learned bishop, meeting the wasted young man of overwhelming spirit, becomes his protector and friend, and it is his authority that later commands Bernard to spare his own body. From this hour Bernard is abbot — a shepherd who will draw the sick and the sinful, the great and the desperate, up the long valley to his door, and send monks out to plant sixty-eight houses across Christendom before he dies.
suggested_refs: Cathedral of Saint-Étienne, Châlons-en-Champagne
William of Champeaux, philosopher and bishop

stops.name: Fontenay — the first daughter of the Bright Valley
stops.campa: Clairvaux, so lately a valley of hunger, begins to swarm with novices, and Bernard sends colonies out to plant new houses in his own image. Fontenay in Burgundy is among the first, its plain church rising bare and perfect after the Cistercian pattern: no towers, no color, no carved beasts, only proportion and light and silence. In Bernard's lifetime sixty-eight abbeys will spring from Clairvaux across France, Italy, Germany, England, Spain, Portugal — a whole reform of the monastic world flowing out of one narrow valley, each daughter a Clairvaux made new.
stops.quote: What is this ridiculous monstrosity in the cloisters, this deformed beauty and beautiful deformity? What are the filthy apes doing there, the fierce lions, the monstrous centaurs? We are more tempted to read in the marble than in our books.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Apologia ad Guillelmum, against ornament in the cloister
suggested_refs: Fontenay Abbey (Abbaye de Fontenay), UNESCO World Heritage Site
The bare Cistercian architecture of the Bernardine plan

segments.name: The Mellifluous Doctor — the Virgin's milk and the loving of God

stops.name: Clairvaux — the Lactation and the amplexus
stops.campa: At prayer before an image of the Mother of God, Bernard implores her — Monstra te esse Matrem, show yourself a Mother. The Virgin answers: from her breast a stream of milk falls upon his lips, and honeyed eloquence flows into him thereafter, so that he is called the Doctor Mellifluous, the honey-flowing teacher. In another wonder the crucified Christ looses His arms from the cross to embrace him — the amplexus. From these graces come his tender preaching of Mary, and men say his tongue is sweeter than the honeycomb because the Mother of God herself has fed it.
stops.quote: In dangers, in doubts, in difficulties, think of Mary, call upon Mary. Following her you will never go astray; with her for guide you will never be weary; with her protecting you, you will never fear.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Homiliae super Missus est (In Praise of the Virgin Mother), Homily II
suggested_refs: The Lactation of Saint Bernard (painting, Ghent master, c.1525)
Alonso Cano, The Vision of Saint Bernard (Prado)

stops.name: Clairvaux — On Loving God (De Diligendo Deo)
stops.campa: At the request of Haimeric, chancellor of the Roman Church, Bernard writes his treatise On Loving God. He answers the question of why God is to be loved, and how much: God is to be loved for His own sake, and the measure of loving Him is to love without measure. He maps four ascending degrees of love — the soul climbing from love of self, to love of God for self's sake, to love of God for God's sake, and at last, rarely, love of self for God's sake. The mellifluous doctor is now a master of the inner life whose words carry across Europe.
stops.quote: You wish me to tell you why and how God should be loved. My answer is that God himself is the reason he is to be loved. As for how he is to be loved, there is to be no limit to that love.
suggested_refs: Manuscripts of De Diligendo Deo
The four degrees of love in Cistercian spirituality
sources: De Diligendo Deo, ed. Cistercian Fathers Series

segments.name: In Praise of the New Knighthood — the pen that founds the Temple

stops.name: Troyes — the Council and the Rule of the Templars
stops.campa: At the Council of Troyes the poor knights of Hugh de Payns, guardians of the pilgrim roads to Jerusalem, are given a Rule and made a religious order of the Church. Bernard's hand is on the drafting; his authority reconciles the sword with the cloister, the monk with the warrior. Here is born the Order of the Temple — the white mantle, the red cross, the vow. From this small synod in Champagne descends the vast Templar power, and the men who will one day burn for it. What Bernard writes at Troyes, Jacques de Molay will die defending on the Île aux Juifs.
suggested_refs: The Latin Rule of the Knights Templar (Council of Troyes, 1129)
Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, Troyes

stops.name: Clairvaux — In Praise of the New Knighthood
stops.campa: For Hugh de Payns, whose knights waver, doubting whether monks may shed blood, Bernard writes the Liber ad milites Templi de laude novae militiae — In Praise of the New Knighthood. He proclaims a new kind of soldier who fights a double war, against flesh and blood and against spiritual evil; who kills not homicide but malicide, slaying not the man but the sin; who cannot lose, for to die in Christ or to slay for Christ is alike gain. He praises them fearless and unwashed, their swords for the wicked, and glorifies the holy places their arms defend.
stops.quote: The knight of Christ, I say, kills with a good conscience and dies with a better. When he dies, he benefits himself; when he kills, he benefits Christ. He does not bear the sword in vain; he is God's minister for the punishment of evildoers.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Liber ad milites Templi de laude novae militiae, III
suggested_refs: Liber ad milites templi de laude novae militiae (manuscript)
The Knights Templar seal, two knights on one horse

segments.name: The Schism and the Hammer — Bernard rules the Church

stops.name: Étampes — the synod that chooses Innocent II
stops.campa: The papacy is torn: two men elected, Innocent II fleeing to France and Anacletus II holding Rome by the Frangipani. King Louis the Fat gathers the bishops of France at Étampes and asks them to judge. They put the whole question into the hands of one man — the abbot of Clairvaux. Bernard, after prayer, declares for Innocent, and his word becomes the verdict of the French Church. From this hour the frail monk is the arbiter of Christendom, carrying the true pope through the courts of kings and the cities of the schism.
suggested_refs: The papal schism of 1130-1138
Pope Innocent II

stops.name: Parthenay (La Coudre) — the Duke of Aquitaine falls before the Host
stops.campa: William X, Duke of Aquitaine, great and violent, clings to the antipope and has driven out bishops loyal to Innocent. Bernard, unable to move him by words, celebrates Mass while the excommunicate duke waits outside the church door. At the consecration Bernard takes up the Body of the Lord upon the paten and comes out to the threshold, his face terrible, and holds the Host toward the armed man, commanding him to submit to God whose servants he despises. William, huge and mail-clad, goes rigid, foams, and falls to the earth as one dead. He rises broken, obeys, and is reconciled; the schism loses its strongest sword.
stops.quote: Here is the Son of the Virgin, the Head and Lord of the Church you persecute. Here is your Judge, at whose name every knee shall bow. Will you despise him as you despise his servants?
stops.quote_source: Vita Prima Bernardi, on the reconciliation of William X
suggested_refs: Église de la Couldre, Parthenay
Vita Prima, Book II, the confrontation with William of Aquitaine

stops.name: Milan — the city won for the pope
stops.campa: Bernard crosses the Alps into Italy for Innocent, reconciling Pisa with Genoa and, hardest of all, the great commune of Milan with the pope. The Milanese pour out to meet him, mob him for the hem of his habit, snatch threads to keep as relics, carry him through the streets. They would make him their archbishop; he flees the honor. In the schism's cities he is peacemaker, envoy, wonder-worker — the little abbot of the Bright Valley moving Italy as a shepherd moves his flock, until Anacletus dies and Rome falls at last to the pope Bernard made.
suggested_refs: Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, Milan
The reconciliation of Milan and the Roman See, 1135

stops.name: Rome — the antipope dead, the schism ended
stops.campa: Bernard comes to Rome itself in the pope's train. Anacletus dies in January 1138 and a rump elects Victor IV in his place, but Bernard, by pleading and the sheer weight of his holiness, persuades Victor to lay down the tiara and submit. The eight-year schism that split kingdoms and armies closes without a war; Innocent II reigns alone. The little abbot of the Bright Valley has healed the deepest wound in Christendom by the labor of his tongue and his feet, city after city, king after king — and then, wanting nothing Rome could give, he turns home to his monks.
suggested_refs: The end of the 1130-1138 papal schism
Antipope Victor IV (Gregorio Conti), who submitted to Bernard

stops.name: Sens — the hammer of Abelard
stops.campa: At the Council of Sens, before archbishops and King Louis VII, Bernard meets Peter Abelard, the sharpest dialectician of the age, whose reason he holds is dissolving the mysteries of the faith. Bernard has already gathered the suspect propositions, letter by letter, and arraigns them one after another. Abelard, seeing not a debate but a tribunal, rises and appeals to Rome rather than answer, and departs. The council condemns his teachings; Bernard's letters to the Curia seal the sentence. The subtle master is silenced, and Bernard stands as the guardian of orthodoxy, the watchdog of Aleth's dream.
stops.quote: Peter Abelard is trying to make void the merit of Christian faith, when he deems himself able by human reason to comprehend God altogether. He ascends to the heavens and descends even to the abyss; nothing may hide from him.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Epistola 190 (to Pope Innocent II), against Abelard
suggested_refs: Cathedral of Saint-Étienne, Sens
The condemned propositions of Peter Abelard, 1141

stops.name: Toulouse and Albi — against the heretics of the Midi
stops.campa: The south of France is stirred by the preaching of Henry of Lausanne, who empties the churches and turns the people against the priesthood; a foretaste of the Cathar tide. Bernard, old and worn, is called down to Languedoc. He preaches at Albi, Toulouse, Verfeil, and the crowds come back to the Church; wonders and healings mark his passage, and the story is told of a possessed woman whose torment he breaks. The Vita Prima closes its record of his life with this journey — the watchdog barking, as Aleth dreamed, against the enemies of the faith to the very end.
stops.quote: The faith is to be produced by persuasion, not imposed by force. Heretics are to be caught rather than driven off — caught, I say, not by arms but by arguments.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Sermon 64 on the Song of Songs, on the heretics
suggested_refs: Sainte-Cécile Cathedral, Albi
Henry of Lausanne and the Henrician heresy

segments.name: The Cross of Vézelay — the Second Crusade and its grief

stops.name: Vézelay — the preaching of the Second Crusade
stops.campa: On the hill of the Magdalene at Vézelay, at Easter, before King Louis VII and Queen Eleanor and a multitude too great for the church, Bernard mounts a wooden platform on the slope and preaches the cross. Edessa has fallen; the pope's bull names Bernard the preacher of the war. He cries out God's offer of pardon to all who take the cross, and the crowd roars 'Crosses! Crosses!' The prepared cloth crosses run out; Bernard tears his own habit into strips to make more. Kings, lords, and thousands are signed with the cross by his hand in a single day.
stops.quote: Take the sign of the cross. At once you shall have indulgence for all the sins which you confess with a contrite heart. The cloth itself sells for little; if it be worn on a faithful shoulder it is worth the kingdom of God.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, crusade preaching and letters (Epistola 363, to the English people)
suggested_refs: Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine, Vézelay
The hillside where Bernard preached, 31 March 1146

stops.name: Mainz — the mob against the Jews turned back
stops.campa: In the Rhineland a renegade monk, Radulf, preaches that the Jews are the enemies within and stirs the mobs to slaughter — at Cologne, Mainz, Worms, Speyer, the old massacres threatening again. Bernard leaves France and comes down the Rhine to stop it. He confronts Radulf at Mainz, silences him, and sends him back to his cloister for breaking obedience and preaching without leave. He forbids the killing in sermon and in letter, teaching that the Jews are living witnesses and must not be touched: whoever lays hands on a Jew lays hands on Jesus himself.
stops.quote: It is an act of Christian piety both to vanquish the proud and to spare the subjected, especially those for whom we have a law and a promise. The Jews are not to be persecuted, killed, or even put to flight.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Epistola 363, on the Jews and the Crusade
suggested_refs: Mainz Cathedral (Mainzer Dom)
Bernard's letters protecting the Rhineland Jews, 1146

stops.name: Frankfurt — the king wavers before the abbot
stops.campa: At the imperial diet in Frankfurt Bernard meets King Conrad III, who holds back from the crusade, judging it folly to leave the Empire for the East. Bernard presses him, but the king will not yield here; the abbot bides, following the court on toward Speyer for the Christmas feast, where he means to lay the whole weight of the Last Judgment on Conrad's conscience. Even now, unbending kings bend to him in the end — the frail monk who commands armies without a sword, moving the crowned heads of Christendom as a shepherd moves a stubborn flock.
suggested_refs: Frankfurt Cathedral (Kaiserdom St. Bartholomäus)
The imperial diet of 1146

stops.name: Constance and Freiburg — the preaching in the tongue he does not speak
stops.campa: Bernard passes up the Rhine through the German lands preaching the cross, though he speaks no German. He preaches in Latin or French; an interpreter renders him after — yet the chroniclers marvel that the crowds are moved more by his untranslated words than by the interpreter's, weeping and taking the cross before they understand a syllable, so that the moving of hearts is laid to God and not to speech. At Constance, Freiburg, Basel and along the road, miracles multiply at his every step — the blind, the lame, the mute healed as he passes.
suggested_refs: Freiburg Minster
Constance Cathedral (Konstanzer Münster)

stops.name: Speyer — Conrad takes the cross, and the Salve Regina
stops.campa: At the imperial cathedral of Speyer, at Christmas, Bernard preaches before Conrad III of Germany, who has refused the cross. He sets before the king the Last Judgment — what will Conrad answer when Christ reproaches him with all His gifts? — and the king, weeping, cries that he will serve. Bernard pins the cross upon Conrad and upon his young nephew Frederick, who will be Barbarossa. Here too the legend is told: as the procession chants the Salve Regina and reaches 'O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria,' Bernard genuflects three times — and Speyer sings the anthem daily in his honor ever after.
stops.quote: O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary.
stops.quote_source: The Salve Regina, the words at which Bernard genuflected at Speyer (traditional addition ascribed to him)
suggested_refs: Speyer Cathedral (Kaiserdom zu Speyer)
The Salve Regina and the legend of Bernard's three genuflections

stops.name: Damascus — the disaster of the crusade
stops.campa: The hosts Bernard raised reach the Holy Land wasted by hunger, ambush, and treachery, and turn against Damascus, a city that might have been a friend. In four days the siege collapses; the kings retreat in shame; the great crusade preached at Vézelay ends in ruin without a battle won. Across Europe the blame falls on Bernard, who promised God's victory. He is stricken with grief and reproach. He will answer that the failure lies not in God's promise but in the sins of the crusaders — yet the wound of it stays on him to the end, the one great enterprise of his life gone to dust.
stops.quote: The sons of the Church have been laid low in the desert; they have perished by the sword or are consumed by famine. We promised peace, and there is no peace; we promised good, and behold trouble — as if we had been rash or fickle.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, De Consideratione, Book II, on the failed Crusade
suggested_refs: The Siege of Damascus, July 1148
Bernard, De Consideratione (written for Pope Eugenius III)

segments.name: The Bright Valley — the Song of Songs and the passing

stops.name: Chartres — chosen to lead a new crusade that never sails
stops.campa: Undaunted by disaster, the leaders gather at Chartres to plan a new crusade to wash out the shame of Damascus, and there they choose Bernard himself to lead it — the preacher to become at last the general of the host. Bernard shrinks from it, an old sick monk no soldier, and writes that he would rather it fell to another; and the enterprise, lacking kings and heart, dies unborn. It is the last flare of the crusading fire he lit at Vézelay, guttering out. He goes home to Clairvaux to the only war he was ever fit for — the war within the soul.
suggested_refs: Chartres Cathedral
The abortive assembly of Chartres, 1150

stops.name: Clairvaux — the Sermons on the Song of Songs
stops.campa: Through the last eighteen years of his life Bernard preaches to his monks upon the Song of Songs — eighty-six sermons, and death takes him before he finishes the second chapter. He reads the bridal poem as the love-story of Christ and the soul, and of Christ and the Church: the kiss of the mouth is the union of the Word with the loving spirit. The old abbot, wasted, worn thin by fasting and disease and the labors of the world, turns wholly to the inner marriage, teaching the seeking soul that runs through the city calling for him whom her soul loves.
stops.quote: Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Who is it that speaks these words? It is the bride. And who is the bride? The soul thirsting for God.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Sermones super Cantica Canticorum, Sermon 7
suggested_refs: Sermones super Cantica Canticorum (86 sermons)
The Cistercian scriptorium of Clairvaux

stops.name: Clairvaux — the death of the abbot
stops.campa: Worn utterly out, ill and grieving, the last of his energy spent healing a feud in the far Rhineland, Bernard comes home to Clairvaux to die. On the twentieth of August, in the sixty-third year of his life and the fortieth of his monastic profession, surrounded by his weeping sons, the mellifluous doctor gives up his spirit. He is buried before the altar of the Lady Chapel of the great church he raised. Sixty-eight abbeys have gone out from his valley; kings, popes, and orders have bent to his word; and the barking white dog of Aleth's dream has kept the house of God his whole life long.
stops.quote: I have loved, O Lord, the beauty of your house, and the place where your glory dwells. In your love I have both lived and now, dying, I commend my spirit to you.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Bernard's last days (Vita Prima, Book V)
suggested_refs: Clairvaux Abbey, site of his tomb
Vita Prima Sancti Bernardi, Book V, on his death

stops.name: Rome (the Lateran) — canonized Saint Bernard
stops.campa: Barely twenty-one years after his death, Pope Alexander III enrolls Bernard among the saints — the first Cistercian to be canonized. His feast is fixed, his tomb a place of pilgrimage, his writings the meat of the whole Church's devotion to Mary and to the loving of God. Centuries later he is named a Doctor of the Church, the Doctor Mellifluous. The abbot of the poor bright valley, who fled every dignity, becomes one of the towering voices of Christendom; and the Rule his pen gave the Templars, and the Holy Land his voice sent them to, outlive him into other men's stories.
suggested_refs: Bull of canonization of Pope Alexander III, 1174
Bernard proclaimed Doctor of the Church (Doctor Mellifluus), 1830
